(OTLK) rallied 12% overnight heading into Monday after the FDA approved Lytenava, the company’s eye drug for treating wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), removing a major regulatory hurdle and putting the spotlight on how much value it can capture as it prepares for a U.S. launch. OTLK stock jumped 6% on Friday to $1.41, snapping two straight sessions of losses. Outlook Therapeutics said on Friday that the FDA approved Lytenava for wet AMD, making it the first and only FDA-approved version of Bevacizumab developed specifically for use in the eye. The decision came ahead of the FDA's July 29 target date and marks a major turnaround after several regulatory setbacks. In December 2025, the FDA rejected Outlook's application and asked for more evidence that the drug was effective. Outlook appealed, and in May the FDA's Office of New Drugs ruled that the existing data were sufficient and that no additional clinical trials were needed. That decision allowed Outlook to resubmit its application in June, leading to Friday's approval. Outlook estimates the U.S. market for anti-VEGF retinal treatments at about $8.5 billion annually, with millions of eye injections given each year. Bevacizumab has been used for more than 20 years in retinal care, including for wet AMD, but largely on an off-label basis. Lytenava stands out because it was developed specifically for injection into the eye and is now FDA-approved for wet AMD. Outlook also expects Lytenava to receive 12 years of U.S. market exclusivity under biologics law. The drug is already approved in the European Union and U.K., with commercial launches underway in Germany, Austria and the U.K. Outlook expects Lytenava to become available to eligible U.S. patients before year-end. The company is expanding reimbursement and patient-support access, building a specialized retina commercial organization and supporting physicians as it prepares for rollout. Economist Paul Krugman warned that President Donald Trump's war against Iran has resulted in refining costs soaring, thereby magnifying the economic impact of higher crude prices. In a note published Thursday, the Nobel Prize-winning economist said crude oil prices hovering around $100 a barrel, combined with an unusually wide gasoline refining "crack spread" worth roughly another $40 per barrel, have left the world facing the economic equivalent of $140 per barrel for oil. “Trump’s gratuitous war on Iran has turned into a remarkable quagmire — remarkable because the only thing keeping the war going is Trump’s vanity. He effectively lost the war in the first few days,” Krugman said. The economist’s comments come amid an escalation in tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he will hold Iran responsible for any subsequent attacks by the Houthi rebels in the Red Sea, after an attack by the group on Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the region earlier this week. He also added that the U.S. will inflict “major military punishment” upon Iran and the Houthis if they attack ships again. Krugman argued that looking at crude oil prices alone understates the economic impact of the conflict. While benchmark crude has climbed to around $100 a barrel, he said the cost of turning crude into gasoline has also surged, with the refining "crack spread" widening to roughly $40 per barrel. Combined, those two components amount to the equivalent of $140 oil, according to Krugman. He said that the large refining margin means consumers are paying far more at the pump than crude prices alone would suggest, making the economic shock significantly more severe despite oil remaining well below historical peaks in nominal terms. The crack spread measures the difference between the price of crude oil and the value of refined products such as gasoline and diesel, serving as a key indicator of refinery profit margins. Crude oil prices eased on Friday after Brent soared past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May 20, 2026. U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures expiring in September were down 2.97%, hovering around $89.45 a barrel. Brent crude futures expiring in September fell 3.13%, hovering around $97.54 a barrel. The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO) and the ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) were down about 2%. Krugman warned that the current energy shock could worsen significantly if the Iran conflict worsens. While he described the present situation as manageable, he said a broader regional war could disrupt energy supplies further and deepen the economic fallout. He also cautioned that any escalation would likely drive up both crude prices and refining margins, amplifying the pressure on consumers and businesses. "Things could get much uglier if this war escalates," Krugman wrote, arguing that the current equivalent of $140 oil may not represent the worst-case scenario. The economist argued that surging energy prices, combined with Trump's new tariffs, could reverse recent progress on inflation and push interest rates higher, intensifying the financial strain on households and businesses. This comes days ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) meeting later this month. content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM, a U.S. oil and gas giant, has an integrated business model spanning upstream operations, refining and trading. The current strength in oil prices is expected to support the company’s profitability in the upstream segment. Oil prices have climbed sharply this week amid escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, including fresh U.S. strikes on Iran. The West Texas Intermediate is trading close to $90 per barrel, while Brent is around $94 per barrel, according to data from oilprice.com. ExxonMobil’s focus on growing production from its advantaged assets in Guyana and the Permian Basin is expected to aid the energy giant’s profits, especially in a favorable oil price environment. The company expects its Permian production to reach 2.5 million oil equivalent barrels per day (Moebd) by the end of this decade, while total production is anticipated to reach 5.5 Moebd. In Guyana, ExxonMobil’s fifth FPSO is on track for startup by year-end, while a final investment decision on the Longtail development is expected soon. In addition, its refining business is poised to benefit from the current volatility in energy markets. While shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz had already tightened product inventories, the recent attacks on Russian refineries have further constrained refining capacity. The outlook for XOM’s Energy Products segment remains positive as lower product inventories and constrained refining capacity continue to support refining margins. This creates a potentially favorable setup across ExxonMobil’s integrated portfolio in the near term. While sustained higher oil prices would primarily benefit its upstream business, supply disruptions and limited refining capacity could provide additional support to downstream margins. However, management warned that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz for a full quarter could significantly affect its Middle East production levels. The integrated platform covers the entire process, from sourcing crude to converting it into refined fuels and distributing the products through its retail and logistics channels. The downstream energy firm has a combined refining capacity of 219,000 barrels per day across Hawaii, Montana, Washington and Wyoming. This integrated setup provides the company with the operational flexibility to capitalize on favorable refining market conditions. Valero Energy VLO is among the largest independent refiners in the United States, with a combined high-complexity throughput capacity of nearly 3 million barrels per day across its refineries. Its refining footprint is heavily concentrated along the U.S. Gulf Coast and the Midcontinent, offering feedstock sourcing flexibility. Moreover, its Gulf Coast access enables it to sell its refined products in high-demand markets and benefit from elevated refining margins and strong international demand for refined products. title: 3 wards and communes in Ho Chi Minh City propose merger but the city has not agreed - Laodong.vn
content: Ho Chi Minh City - Khanh Hoi Ward, Xom Chieu Ward and Long Son commune proposed to merge with adjacent localities but have not been approved by the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee. The information is stated in Official Dispatch No. 1168/TTr-UBND of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee sent to the Standing Committee of the Party Committee of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee on the results of reviewing the plan for arranging commune-level administrative units in the area. According to the report, there are 3 out of a total of 168 wards, communes, and special zones proposing arrangement plans, including Khanh Hoi ward, Xom Chieu ward, and Long Son commune. Xom Chieu Ward People's Committee has a natural area of 1.94km2 (not meeting the prescribed standards), a population of 53,067 people, and a density of about 27,354 people/km2. At the conference to review and evaluate the operation of the locality, the People's Committee of Xom Chieu ward proposed to merge Khanh Hoi ward, Vinh Hoi ward and Xom Chieu ward into a new administrative unit. According to local authorities, this plan aims to ensure the continuity of urban space, while also being suitable for the development orientation of the Saigon riverside area. Similarly, Khanh Hoi ward has an area of 1.06km2 (not meeting the prescribed standards), a population of 74,214 people, and a density of about 70,013 people/km2. This ward proposes 2 options. The first option is to merge Khanh Hoi, Vinh Hoi and Xom Chieu into a new ward. The second option is to merge the above 3 wards with another adjacent administrative unit to ensure criteria for area and expand development space. However, the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee believes that if Khanh Hoi, Vinh Hoi and Xom Chieu are only merged, the new unit will have an area of about 4.18km2, still not meeting the minimum standard of 5.5km2 according to Resolution 112/2025/UBTVQH15. In addition, the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee believes that Khanh Hoi and Xom Chieu wards have not yet consulted or exchanged opinions with adjacent localities on the proposed plan. The two wards have also not comprehensively assessed the irrationalities arising after one year of operating the 2-level local government model to serve as a basis for proposing adjustments. According to the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, among 165 commune-level administrative units proposing to maintain the status quo, 46 wards have not met the area standards. However, these localities have specifically assessed the operation process and believe that maintaining the status quo does not cause irrationalities. Therefore, the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee has not agreed with the merger plan proposed by Khanh Hoi and Xom Chieu wards, and at the same time proposed to temporarily maintain the existing administrative units. Another case is Long Son commune. This is a unit that meets the standards for natural area with 56.5km2, but does not meet the standards for population size, with 24,684 people. On August 13, the Standing Committee of the Long Son Commune Party Committee agreed to study 3 options for arranging administrative units and proposed to choose the option of merging Long Son with Tan Hai ward to form a new administrative unit. However, this plan did not receive consensus from relevant localities. On August 17, the Standing Committee of the Long Son Commune Party Committee sent a document to the Standing Committee of the Tan Hai Ward Party Committee requesting consideration of the merger plan. On August 20, Tan Hai ward had a written reply, in which it agreed to continue to maintain the stability of the administrative unit of Tan Hai ward. Thus, Tan Hai ward does not agree with the merger proposal of Long Son commune. The Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee also believes that the report of Long Son commune has only stopped at evaluating and analyzing 3 arrangement options, and has not fully selected and completed a specific option. On the other hand, the merger plan of Long Son and Tan Hai has not been agreed upon between localities, is not complete and has not proven the urgency of adjustment. Therefore, the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee proposed to temporarily maintain Long Son commune and Tan Hai ward, and not to adjust the administrative boundaries between the two localities. title: Two Utility Dividend Plays Are Quietly Beating XOM, CVX On Yield Amid Iran-Driven Oil Rally — Does Retail Know? - Stocktwits
content: Energy companies have made a comeback as strong market performers amid the recent conflict in the Strait of Hormuz and rising oil prices. While the top energy companies have delivered double-digit price growth so far in 2026, two smaller energy utility companies have outperformed them in dividend returns. Duke Energy Corp. (DUK) and WEC Energy Group Inc. (WEC) are among the top dividend stocks in the market, according to a recent report from Morningstar. DUK stock has provided the highest dividend yield in the group at 3.6% as of Sept. 2, according to data from Fiscal.ai. WEC stock comes close, offering a dividend yield of 3.5%. Meanwhile, among the top energy stocks, Chevron Corp. (CVX) has a dividend yield of 3.3%, while rivals Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and ConocoPhillips (COP) provide dividend returns of 2.5% each. Morningstar has a fair value estimate of $131 for DUK stock, implying nearly 9% upside from its last close. The analyst has a ‘Narrow’ Economic Moat Rating on the shares, but projects a forward dividend yield of 3.61%. Morningstar said in a note that Duke operates in constructive regulatory environments where much of its regulated business operates and has better-than-average economic fundamentals in its key regions, according to senior analyst Andrew Bischof. The company’s liquidity position and cash flow generation provide confidence that it can maintain and increase its dividend. Morningstar expects a 5% annual dividend growth from the company over time. As of June 30, 2026, the company generated $4.27 billion in operating cash flow. Duke Energy had a balance of $850 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash at the end of the period, compared to $442 million in the previous year’s comparable quarter. As per Morningstar, WEC Energy is one of the best dividend stocks to buy in the market. The analyst has a fair value estimate of $116 for WEC stock, implying nearly 10% upside from its last close. The analyst has a ‘Narrow’ Economic Moat Rating on the shares, but projects a forward dividend yield of 3.59%. Morningstar said WEC has built a narrow economic moat through service-territory monopolies and efficient-scale advantages, adding that management is targeting a 65%-70% dividend payout ratio. The analyst expects dividend growth to average 6.5%. As of June 30, 2026, the company generated $2.21 billion in operating cash flow. WEC had a balance of $95.9 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash at the end of the period, compared to $69.2 million in the previous year’s comparable quarter. Broadcom Inc.’s AI chip business is showing little sign of slowing down, with the semiconductor giant expecting revenue from its AI chips to double in each of the next two years as demand from customers including Anthropic and OpenAI accelerates. The Palo Alto, California-based company expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach about $115 billion in fiscal 2027, up from roughly $58 billion expected in 2026, CEO Hock Tan said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. The company sees another doubling to $230 billion in fiscal 2028, underscoring the strength of its custom AI accelerator and networking chip business. “In 2027, we have secured the supply to again double AI revenue to approximately $115 billion. Our demand actually exceeds this outlook, and we will work to improve supply,” Tan said. “In 2028… we have line of sight for fiscal 2028 AI semiconductor revenue growth to again double to $230 billion. Here again, we have secured the supply to meet this outlook.” Despite the strong outlook, Broadcom’s fourth-quarter revenue forecast, which implies 93% growth, came in below Wall Street’s expectations, sending AVGO shares 1.3% lower in overnight trading late Wednesday. The comments highlight how Broadcom has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom beyond Nvidia. Its custom accelerators, or XPUs, are increasingly being adopted by major AI companies looking to build their own chips. AI chip sales more than tripled to $16.7 billion in the third quarter, lifting Broadcom's total revenue 86% to $29.59 billion, beating estimates of $29.36 billion. Adjusted profit came in at $3.32 ​per share, compared with estimates of $3.24. Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom’s largest XPU customer next year, with the AI startup planning to deploy another 5 gigawatts of Broadcom-designed TPU v8i chips in 2027 and an additional 10 gigawatts in 2028. OpenAI is also expected to become a major customer, with Broadcom seeing a path for the ChatGPT maker to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of its next-generation Jalapeno XPU in 2028. “These two guys, Anthropic and OpenAI, I mean, these are… it’s like you have two geniuses in the middle of outer Mongolia. They need to go to college to fulfill their potential,” Tan said, suggesting that while both companies have enormous potential, they need access to Broadcom’s chips and infrastructure (“college”) to fully realize it. “We do what we can to help them, and part of it is creating sources of financing to help these companies with the leading-edge frontier models in the world be able to play in the same playing field and be able to offer these great technology products to the world,” he added. Broadcom has secured supplies for wafers, substrates and memory needed to meet its 2027 and 2028 AI revenue targets. The company also plans to begin deploying its Singapore substrate facility in fiscal 2027 to ease a key supply bottleneck. Moor Insights & Strategy CEO and analyst Patrick Moorhead said Broadcom delivered a “strong, but not flawless” third quarter, arguing that the key takeaway was its AI execution rather than the modest revenue beat. He pointed to Broadcom’s $16.7 billion in Q3 AI revenue and $21.7 billion Q4 outlook as evidence that the company is successfully converting its AI backlog into sales. Moorhead also highlighted Broadcom’s broader AI infrastructure advantage, spanning custom XPU co-design, Ethernet switching, SerDes, optics, packaging and foundry access, but cautioned that the results “do not prove broad NVIDIA displacement.” “The wrinkle is software, and the release does not resolve customer concentration, Google multisourcing, bookings conversion, AI networking mix, first-generation XPU yields or the fiscal 2027 AI bridge,” he said. Future Fund Managing Director Gary Black noted the improvement in AVGO stock after-hours “as investors responded favorably to the company’s AI rev growth guidance”. “As the AI Rev strength becomes clearer to investors, I expect the stock to recover somewhat,” he said. AVGO was the top trending ticker on Stocktwits at the time of writing, with the retail sentiment for the stock turning ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ the previous day. “$AVGO Broadcom just posted the most massive financial results in company history — bears can say whatever they want — the share price will go higher regardless,” a trader said. Another wrote: “$AVGO it takes time for the earnings results and outlook to filter into the market; this forward outlook is insane… The stock is too cheap, just like Nvidia.  It’s going higher.” AVGO stock declined in the two sessions leading up to the Q3 report and is up a mere 6.5% year to date. In comparison, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) has gained over 65% over the same period. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) snapped a three-session losing streak on Wednesday after the space company completed its 94th Electron mission, with investors appearing to look past a regulatory filing disclosing an $8.77 million share sale by its CFO. RKLB stock rose 1% on Wednesday to finish the session at $63.10. However, the shares remain on track for their fourth consecutive weekly decline. Rocket Lab launched the “Owl Around The World” mission from its Mahia launch complex in New Zealand after high winds forced the company to postpone the flight twice. The Electron rocket successfully deployed Synspective’s latest StriX satellite into a 575-kilometer low-Earth orbit. The satellite uses synthetic aperture radar to capture images of the Earth’s surface regardless of cloud cover, weather conditions or daylight. Rocket Lab also developed a payload fairing specifically tailored to the dimensions of the StriX satellite. The company said Electron remains the world’s most frequently launched small orbital rocket. The mission marked Rocket Lab’s 15th launch of 2026 and 11th successful mission for Synspective, extending its perfect launch record for the Japanese satellite operator. The two companies began working together in 2020 as Synspective sought to build out its constellation of radar-imaging satellites. Another 16 dedicated Electron missions for Synspective remain booked through 2030, giving Rocket Lab a pipeline of repeat business from Synspective. The order book was expanded in June when Synspective signed on for 17 additional Electron launches. Wednesday’s flight was the first mission completed under the expanded commitment. Rocket Lab’s previous Electron flight, its 93rd overall, deployed another Earth-observation satellite for Japanese customer iQPS in August. Nine more dedicated launches for iQPS are booked through 2030. Meanwhile, a fresh regulatory filing from late Wednesday showed that Rocket Lab CFO Adam Spice intends to sell 140,157 shares with an aggregate market value of about $8.77 million. Spice acquired the shares on Wednesday through the exercise of stock options. The proposed transaction was arranged under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan adopted on June 3. Spice also sold 56,303 Rocket Lab shares across three transactions in August, generating combined gross proceeds of about $4.45 million, the filing showed. The newly proposed sale represents about 0.02% of Rocket Lab’s 598.4 million outstanding shares. Additionally, Rocket Lab director Merline Saintil also filed a Form 4 late Wednesday covering the transfer of 261,903 shares to her revocable living trust. After the transfer, Saintil directly owned 2,482 shares and indirectly held 261,903 shares through the trust, according to the filing. Executives have signaled that a final decision on sanctioning the largest phase of the Nigeria development could arrive within the coming year, contingent on regulatory alignment and continued progress on commercial terms with the host government and joint-venture partners. Beyond West Africa, ExxonMobil's growth story continues to center on two core regions: the offshore Guyana development, where production has scaled rapidly across multiple floating platforms, and the Permian Basin, where the company holds one of the largest acreage positions among major operators following its earlier combination with Pioneer Natural Resources. In the Permian, ExxonMobil has emphasized efficiency gains from longer laterals and simultaneous operations, arguing that unit costs across the basin have moved meaningfully lower even as overall activity levels have held steady. ExxonMobil declared its latest quarterly payout to stockholders, continuing a streak of consecutive annual increases that stretches back decades. The steady payout has long been viewed as a defining feature of ExxonMobil's stockholder-return framework, distinguishing it from peers that have historically leaned more heavily on variable or special distributions. While upstream volumes tend to dominate headlines, ExxonMobil's downstream and chemicals operations provide an important counterweight when crude prices soften. Refining margins have remained supportive this year, aided by steady demand for gasoline and diesel across domestic and export markets, while the chemicals segment has benefited from a gradual recovery in industrial demand after a prolonged stretch of oversupply across the petrochemical complex. The company has continued channeling capital into advanced recycling and lower-carbon technologies within its chemicals and product-solutions businesses, framing these projects as a way to capture emerging demand for circular plastics and specialty products without diverting significant capital away from its core hydrocarbon operations. A recurring theme across ExxonMobil's recent communications has been structural cost reduction. The company has pointed to multi-billion-dollar annual savings achieved through process efficiency, procurement improvements and organizational changes implemented over the past several years. Management has argued that these savings are largely structural rather than cyclical, meaning they should persist even if crude prices were to soften from current levels. This cost discipline has become a central plank of the company's pitch, alongside its growth pipeline in Guyana, the Permian and West Africa. Executives have repeatedly emphasized that the combination of lower costs and higher-margin production growth should support cash generation across a wide range of commodity-price environments in the years ahead. Coverage teams have also pointed to the company's balance-sheet strength as a differentiator, noting that ExxonMobil entered the current cycle with comparatively low leverage relative to many peers, giving it flexibility to continue funding both its dividend and its capital program without leaning heavily on additional borrowing. The broader backdrop for ExxonMobil's advance has been a steady firming in global crude benchmarks, with both domestic and international grades trading well above the lows seen earlier in the cycle. Traders have pointed to disciplined supply management among major producing nations, alongside steady demand growth from transportation and petrochemical end-markets, as reasons the complex has held together despite periodic bouts of macro uncertainty. Refined-product cracks have also remained firm across most regions, supporting margins for ExxonMobil's downstream network even as crude costs have climbed. The combination of firmer upstream realizations and resilient downstream margins has given the company a comparatively balanced earnings profile relative to peers that skew more heavily toward either upstream or downstream operations. ExxonMobil has continued to emphasize its balance-sheet strength as a defining feature of its broader strategy, noting that comparatively low leverage gives it room to fund its capital program, its dividend and opportunistic moves such as the Nigeria expansion without leaning heavily on additional borrowing. Executives have framed this financial flexibility as a structural advantage relative to peers carrying heavier debt loads. The company's cash position has also supported continued spending on lower-carbon initiatives, including carbon capture and hydrogen projects that management has framed as longer-cycle growth avenues distinct from the core hydrocarbon business. While these ventures remain a modest share of overall spending, executives have pointed to early commercial agreements as evidence of building demand. Set against fellow integrated majors, ExxonMobil has generally been viewed as carrying a broader and more diversified growth pipeline, spanning Guyana, the Permian Basin and now an expanding position in West Africa. Coverage teams have often contrasted this breadth with peers that lean more heavily on a single region or basin for incremental volume growth. That diversification has also been cited as a reason ExxonMobil's shares have tracked closely with the broader energy group rather than diverging sharply in either direction, since strength or softness in any single region tends to be offset by performance elsewhere across the global portfolio. Beyond crude and refined products, ExxonMobil has continued to expand its footprint in natural gas, including liquefied natural gas ventures aimed at capturing demand growth tied to power generation and industrial use across international markets. Executives have pointed to rising electricity demand linked to data-center and manufacturing activity as a structural tailwind for gas-focused investing over the coming years. The company's gas positions, spanning both domestic shale basins and international liquefaction projects, have been framed as a complementary growth avenue to its oil-weighted upstream portfolio, providing exposure to a fuel source that has drawn growing attention amid broader shifts in global energy demand patterns. As ExxonMobil advances its Nigeria commitments, the company has continued to work closely with regulators and host-government partners on terms related to domestic value retention, local content requirements and environmental compliance. These discussions have been described as a routine part of large-scale deepwater project development in the region, rather than a departure from established practice. Industry observers have noted that securing durable, long-term fiscal terms remains a prerequisite for sanctioning projects of this scale, and that ExxonMobil's continued engagement in Nigeria reflects confidence that the commercial framework will ultimately support a positive final decision on the largest phase of the development. Global demand for refined products has remained resilient this year, with gasoline and diesel consumption staying firm across most major economies even as electrification trends continue to reshape long-term demand expectations for road transportation fuels. ExxonMobil has pointed to steady jet-fuel demand tied to continued growth in international air travel as a particularly supportive trend for its downstream network. Petrochemical demand has also shown signs of gradual recovery after a prolonged period of oversupply weighed on margins across the industry, with ExxonMobil citing improving operating rates at its chemical facilities as evidence that the broader cycle may be turning in a more favorable direction for producers with scale advantages. Looking ahead, market participants will be watching for further updates on the Nigeria sanctioning process, continued production ramp-up in Guyana and any commentary on capital spending plans for the coming year. The company's next scheduled communication with the market will likely include updated guidance on production volumes and capital allocation priorities. Broader crude-price dynamics, including OPEC+ supply decisions and global demand trends, will remain the dominant swing factor for the stock in the near term. With energy names leading much of the market's advance this year, ExxonMobil's scale, diversified portfolio and cost position continue to place it at the center of that conversation among major integrated operators.  moved back into the market's line of sight as opened, after crude prices vaulted higher on news of fresh strikes on Iranian sites and attacks on two tankers near one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints. Brent grades pushed well above the levels that had prevailed through the summer, and the move was sharp enough to drag equity benchmarks lower while lifting bond yields on inflation concerns. For the largest American energy producer, the escalation cuts both ways. Higher crude realisations lift the value of every barrel lifted from the Permian Basin, Guyana and the North Sea, yet the company also carries operations and equity interests in the Middle East that have been directly interrupted by the crisis. How those two effects net out has become one of the defining questions around the business this year. The immediate trigger was military escalation. Strikes on Iranian sites followed attacks on commercial tankers in the waterway that carries a very large share of seaborne crude and condensate, and the combination reignited concerns that had been simmering since the conflict began earlier in the year. The chokepoint has been substantially closed for months. Transit counts have collapsed to a small fraction of the daily crossings recorded before the conflict, leaving a vast volume of daily flow either rerouted, delayed or simply removed from the market. Producers with export routes that bypass the strait have gained relative importance, while those dependent on it have seen liftings interrupted. Market commentary through had settled around the view that crude would remain supported at elevated levels until diplomatic progress emerged, with Middle Eastern production not expected to return to pre-conflict volumes until well into next year. The events at the start of pushed prices past even that supported band, and the speed of the move suggested the market had grown complacent about the possibility of further escalation. Freight economics compound the effect. Insurance premiums for vessels operating in the region have climbed, crews have become harder to secure, and rerouting adds voyage days. Those costs sit on top of the crude price itself and feed through to refined product pricing in importing regions. Management has been explicit that disruption in the Middle East reduced overall output during the second quarter, and equally explicit that growth from the Permian Basin and Guyana largely offset the shortfall. Excluding the interrupted barrels, upstream production reached its highest level in more than two decades, which is a striking claim for a business of this vintage. That resilience is a product of portfolio design rather than luck. Over the past several years the company has concentrated capital on a smaller number of very large, low-cost developments while divesting assets that sat higher on the cost curve. The effect is a portfolio that generates cash across a wide band of crude prices and is geographically weighted toward the Western Hemisphere. Cost discipline reinforces that. The company has reported cumulative structural cost savings running into the tens of billions of dollars since the start of its efficiency programme, with further savings added during the first half of this year. Structural savings differ from cyclical cuts because they change the cost base rather than deferring spending, and they compound as volumes grow. Cash generation has followed. Operating cash flow and free cash flow through the second quarter were both substantial, funding capital spending, dividends and share reduction programmes simultaneously. That capacity is what allows a producer to keep investing through a volatile stretch rather than pulling back and losing momentum. The Stabroek Block offshore Guyana has become one of the most consequential deepwater developments anywhere. Output from the block now runs close to nine hundred thousand barrels a day, produced through a sequence of floating production, storage and offloading vessels, each added as a discrete project. The fifth vessel began producing during the current year, adding roughly a quarter of a million barrels a day of capacity. A sixth development is under construction with similar capacity expected before the end of next year, and a seventh is progressing toward the end of the decade with somewhat smaller capacity. Two further projects sit behind those in the development queue. What makes the block unusual is the combination of scale, reservoir quality and unit cost. Development costs per barrel have come in low by deepwater standards, partly because each successive vessel benefits from lessons learned on the last, and partly because the reservoirs deliver high flow rates. The result is a growth engine that adds volume in large, discrete steps rather than through incremental drilling. The company has also flagged natural gas from Guyana as the next frontier, alongside applications to expand operations further. Gas development would broaden the resource base beyond crude and support domestic power generation ambitions in the host country. Onshore American shale provides the second growth pillar. Permian output has set records, running above one and three-quarter million oil-equivalent barrels a day, and the company has described a compound growth path continuing through the end of the decade. The Permian position combines legacy acreage with a large corporate acquisition that added contiguous, undeveloped inventory in the Midland Basin. Contiguity matters because it allows longer horizontal laterals, shared infrastructure and more efficient water handling, all of which lower unit costs. Technology has become a differentiator here. The company has pushed automation across drilling and completion operations, applied advanced recovery techniques to lightweight crude, and used data systems to optimise well spacing and fracture design. Shale is a manufacturing business at scale, and marginal efficiency gains repeat across thousands of wells. Short cycle times are the strategic value. A shale barrel can be brought online within months, whereas a deepwater project takes years. Keeping both in one portfolio gives a producer the ability to respond to price signals without abandoning long-horizon developments. Earlier in the year the board recommended moving the company's domicile from New Jersey to Texas, and the redomiciliation merger became effective at the start of. Each outstanding share was exchanged one for one into shares of a newly formed Texas parent, and ownership percentages were unchanged. The stock continued trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the same ticker throughout, so the change was legal and administrative rather than commercial. The practical rationale relates to corporate governance frameworks and the concentration of the company's operations and workforce in Texas, where its headquarters sits. For anyone following oil and gas stocks, the point worth noting is that the operating business, asset base and reporting continuity were unaffected. The name of the parent entity changed, but the underlying enterprise did not. Upstream production is only part of the enterprise. The company operates one of the largest refining systems in the world, alongside a substantial chemicals business producing polymers, performance products and specialty materials. Downstream economics move differently from upstream ones. When crude spikes, refining margins can compress if product prices lag, though disrupted supply of refined products can push margins the other way. Chemical margins depend on the spread between feedstock costs and product prices, and cheap American natural gas liquids have historically given domestic crackers an advantage over naphtha-based competitors elsewhere. The company has been shifting the product mix toward higher-value performance materials rather than commodity grades, which reduces sensitivity to the chemical cycle. Spending on lubricants, advanced recycling and specialty polymers all point in that direction. Integration provides a further buffer. A producer that also refines and manufactures captures value at several points along the chain, which smooths results relative to a pure-play at either end. Capital allocation at this scale is a long-horizon exercise, and the company has been consistent about the framework it applies. Spending is directed toward developments that generate acceptable economics at conservative price assumptions rather than at prevailing spot levels, which is what allows programmes to continue when prices fall rather than being cancelled at the worst moment. Capital expenditure through the first half of the year ran into the low tens of billions of dollars, weighted toward Guyana, the Permian Basin, downstream upgrades and the lower carbon unit. Management has noted that its annual spending materially exceeds that of its nearest international peer, which reflects both the size of the project queue and a deliberate choice to keep building through the cycle. Balance sheet strength underpins that approach. A conservative debt position gives a producer the ability to sustain distributions and capital programmes through a downturn without resorting to asset sales at depressed prices. It also allows opportunistic acquisitions when weaker operators become available, which is how several of the largest recent transactions in the sector came about. The distribution record forms the other half of the picture. Dividends have been maintained and increased over a long stretch, and share count reduction programmes have run alongside them. Together those absorb a substantial share of free cash flow, which is why the ability to fund growth simultaneously depends so heavily on the cost base. A disruption that removes crude from the market also disturbs the flow of refined products, and refining systems located away from the affected region gain relative value. Gulf Coast refineries with access to domestic crude and cheap natural gas for process heat are comparatively insulated from the freight and insurance costs weighing on cargoes moving out of the affected waterway. Crude slate flexibility matters here. A refinery configured to process a wide range of grades can substitute feedstocks as availability shifts, whereas a plant optimised for a single heavy sour grade struggle when that grade becomes scarce. Complex refining systems with deep conversion capacity generally keep an advantage during a supply shock for exactly that reason. Product export capability adds another dimension. American refiners have become substantial exporters of diesel and gasoline, and when disrupted supply lifts product prices in importing regions, that export position captures the differential. The interplay between crude cost and product realisation is what determines whether a refining system amplifies or offsets the effect of a crude spike. Alongside the core business, the company has built a dedicated unit focused on carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, lithium and lower-emission fuels. The commercial logic rests on applying existing subsurface, project management and molecule-handling expertise to adjacent markets. Carbon capture is furthest advanced, with contracts signed to transport and store emissions from industrial customers along the Gulf Coast. Hydrogen and ammonia projects are progressing where regulatory support and industrial demand coincide. Lithium extraction from brine draws on the same subsurface capabilities used in conventional production. These ventures remain small relative to the core business, and their pace depends heavily on regulatory frameworks and customer commitments. They are best understood as optionality built on existing competence rather than a pivot away from hydrocarbons. The whole sector has been reshaped by the shipping crisis. Producers with export routes outside the affected region have gained pricing power, refiners have adjusted crude slates to reflect availability, and shipping rates have risen sharply. Importing economies in Asia and Europe have absorbed the largest share of the disruption. Producer group dynamics have also changed. Spare capacity concentrated in the affected region cannot easily reach the market while transit is constrained, which blunts the usual mechanism by which supply responds to price. That is one reason prices have stayed firm despite demand concerns tied to slower global growth. Elsewhere, exploration activity has picked up in West Africa, South America and the eastern Mediterranean as producers seek barrels away from geopolitical flashpoints. Capital that had been directed toward short-cycle shale is being rebalanced toward longer-life international projects with diversified export routes. Cost inflation is one. Rig rates, vessel charters, steel and skilled labour have all become more expensive during periods of high activity, and service sector capacity is finite. Producers that locked in contracts early carry an advantage over those contracting in the spot market. Volatility is another. A price environment driven by military events rather than supply and demand fundamentals is inherently unstable, and a diplomatic breakthrough could unwind a large part of the current premium quickly. Planning capital programmes against such a backdrop requires conservative assumptions. Regulatory and permitting timelines add a third layer, particularly for projects requiring environmental approvals in multiple jurisdictions. Long-cycle developments must clear those hurdles years before first production, which places a premium on portfolio depth. Several markers stand out. Progress on the Guyana development queue, particularly the sixth vessel, will determine how quickly growth volumes arrive. title: Striking Oil: How the U.S. Play for Venezuela Fuels Supermajors - MarketBeat
content:
Middle Eastern supply-chain risks are adding urgency to renewed U.S. engagement with Venezuela’s vast energy reserves, potentially creating new opportunities for domestic supermajors with the scale and expertise to participate. As capital flows aggressively into this geopolitical divergence play, peak operational leverage and fortified balance sheets position key upstream companies for significant upside. Investors watching global Brent prices spike on war fears might be missing the underlying domestic energy play. A structural shift in physical energy markets is underway, one that bypasses traditional, conflict-prone supply routes and anchors directly into the world's largest oil reserves. The geopolitical risk premium on oil may be climbing rapidly, but the true wealth generation is happening behind closed doors through foreign policy maneuvering. Understanding the fundamentals behind this transition illuminates a highly lucrative, multi-year runway for integrated energy equities. The escalation in the Middle East is rewriting the risk models for global energy supply. With fresh airstrikes shifting the geopolitical risk premium, the vulnerability of the Strait of Hormuz is causing Western powers to adopt a strategic hedge. The unpriced catalyst driving recent market momentum is the U.S. Department of War's active pursuit of an approximately 35% stake in Venezuelan oil rights through third-party intermediaries. This maneuver effectively opens a pool of Latin American reserves to backfill depleted domestic Strategic Petroleum Reserves. For investors, this creates an asymmetric risk-to-reward profile. Global oil prices remain elevated due to geopolitical instability, while select domestic companies gain government-backed extraction rights just south of the border. The sector has already seen a sharp repricing to the upside, but the cash flows generated by this new extraction mandate are only beginning to materialize. Investors pricing in standard cyclical commodity fluctuations may be underestimating the long-term cash flow stability provided by this federal backing of foreign heavy crude. When evaluating the macro landscape, access to physical commodities takes precedence over temporary pricing dynamics. The integration of Venezuelan crude into the U.S. refining ecosystem is not a short-term trade; it represents a realignment of energy dependence, shielding domestic producers from overseas bottlenecks. Executing a state-sponsored extraction mandate requires an impenetrable balance sheet and vast logistical networks. Chevron Corporation NYSE: CVX and ExxonMobil NYSE: XOM are uniquely positioned to leverage these new global reserves and could be real beneficiaries of this foreign policy pivot. Chevron Corporation recently reported a 57.4% year-over-year revenue surge, posting $6.06 earnings per share against a $5.55 consensus. This earnings beat demonstrates peak operational leverage right before a transformative international expansion. Chevron's stock price is up around 39% year-to-date, currently trading near $210, backed by a resilient 3.4% dividend yield and a $419 billion market capitalization. Trading at a price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 20, the valuation remains highly competitive given the impending revenue streams from new Latin American fields. ExxonMobil generated an imposing $114.53 billion in quarterly revenue, boasting a trailing return on equity of about 13.14%. The sheer scale of these operations entirely eclipses the minor domestic political friction currently making headlines. While the administration publicly presses refiners on rising consumer gas prices and excludes key executives from domestic policy meetings, the geopolitical reality dictates that ExxonMobil and Chevron Corporation are among the few operators with the capital expenditure runway to handle a Venezuelan infrastructure overhaul. Extracting heavy crude from neglected Latin American fields requires substantial upfront capital and elite technical retrofitting. This necessity brings oilfield service providers sharply into focus, making Halliburton Company NYSE: HAL a critical name in this geopolitical equation. When supermajors secure foreign extraction rights, they often outsource the highly specialized infrastructure recovery to proven service titans. Halliburton Company operates with a healthy 18.71% return on equity and a stable net margin of about 7.16%. The stock has risen over 30% this year, trading near $37, yet Wall Street consensus maintains a price target around $43.10, suggesting that healthy upside potential remains. Service providers capture the highest-margin contracts during the initial phases of infrastructure revitalization. Halliburton Company is positioned to absorb future capital expenditure deployed by Chevron Corporation and ExxonMobil. As the physical fields in Venezuela are brought back online, proprietary drilling technology, cementing services, and reservoir consulting will become non-negotiable line items for the supermajors. This could create a highly insulated revenue stream for Halliburton Company, safely detached from the day-to-day volatility of oil prices. Service contracts are locked in regardless of short-term crude fluctuations, offering a defensive posture within a high-beta sector. The synchronized momentum across integrated oil and energy services is not just a typical commodity-cycle peak. It represents a repricing of geopolitical energy security. The rapid year-to-date gains across Chevron Corporation, ExxonMobil, and Halliburton Company align with the new Venezuelan extraction catalyst. Those looking to capitalize on this divergence play might consider adding these equities to a watchlist, waiting for minor market pullbacks before taking a position. That structural difference has become more visible during the current stretch of crude volatility, as pure-play producers have tended to see sharper percentage swings in their share prices than integrated peers. That dynamic looks set to persist for as long as the situation around the Strait of Hormuz remains unresolved. In plain English, that means recent buyers have been willing to pay more than the average price of the last 20 and 50 sessions, which is typically a sign that momentum is still leaning upward.Track Market Trends There is no new MA-cross, so the message from the moving averages is steady rather than dramatic. The SMA20 slope of 0.74% over 5 days reinforces that the nearer trend is still rising, but the absence of a fresh crossover suggests the move is more of a continuation than a new technical regime. Price is also positioned at about 89% of the 20-hour range, with the stock trading between 151.63 support and 166.15 resistance. That placement tells you XOM is pressing toward the top of the recent band, where gains often become harder to extend unless volume confirms the push. The stock remains below its 3-month high of 168.64, so the market has not yet fully reclaimed the upper boundary of the broader recent range. The momentum picture is more mixed than the price trend. The RSI at 61.0 is neutral, which means the stock is not stretched into overbought territory and still has room to advance without immediately looking overheated. At the same time, neutrality also means the oscillator is not providing a strong acceleration signal on its own. The Stochastic %K at 67.3 and %D at 39.9 points to improving short-term momentum, but not yet a fully confirmed thrust. Stochastic compares the latest price to its recent range; when it rises ahead of price confirmation, it can hint that buyers are reasserting control, though the signal is still early here. The more important caution comes from MACD. XOM’s MACD at 2.627 remains above zero, which generally means the broader trend is still positive, but it sits below the signal line at 3.172 and the histogram at -0.545 is negative. That combination means upside momentum has slowed even as the price itself has stayed firm. Last trade volume of 11,381,800 was only 0.8× the 20-day average of 14,261,315, while OBV is falling. OBV, or on-balance volume, tracks whether volume is flowing into gains or into declines; a falling line during a price rise often means the rally is not being broadly supported.
